Okay, this is a tricky deferred acceptance problem. My values for w and z are the same ($78), and my values for x and y are the same ($66). However, my *priority* at w and y are higher (rank 1) than at x and z (rank 2).

The key piece of information is that "most applicants seem to favor y > x > w > z". This means y will be *very* competitive. Given my high rank at y (1), I absolutely need to list y as my first choice. If I don't, I'm almost guaranteed to not get in.

Now, between w and z, I'm indifferent based on my value. However, I have a higher priority at w (rank 1) than at z (rank 2). Since many applicants favor y > x > w > z, w will likely be less competitive than z. Therefore, I should list w second to take advantage of my higher priority there. This increases my chances of getting into *a* good school.

Finally, I'll list z third, and x last. While x and z are valued the same to me, x is more popular overall, and my rank at z is higher than at x.

This strategy aims to maximize my chances of getting into either w or y, given the preferences of other students. Listing y first is critical, and listing w second leverages my priority at that school.
reasoning.Student B:
Okay, this is a classic deferred acceptance problem. My personal values are z > w > x > y. However, I'm told most students prefer y > x > w > z. This is *crucially* important.

If I rank according to my values (z > w > x > y), I'm likely to be rejected repeatedly. Everyone else wants y first, and I'm putting it last. I'll quickly burn through my preferences and end up unmatched.

My high priority at school 'x' is a significant advantage. If I can get into 'x', I likely will. But getting into 'x' depends on other students' rankings. Since most students rank 'y' higher than 'x', 'x' will likely have spaces available after the first round.

My priority at 'z' is also high, but it's a less reliable option because almost no one wants it. I need to consider how many students will rank 'z' at all.

My strategy needs to be to leverage my high priority at 'x' while still keeping 'z' as a fallback. I will rank 'x' first, hoping to secure a match. Then, I'll rank 'z' second, recognizing its high value to me, and hoping that if 'x' doesn't work out, my priority at 'z' will be enough. I'll then rank 'w' and 'y' last, since I value them the least and everyone else values 'y' highly. This puts me in a position to potentially get 'x' or 'z', and avoids being last in line for 'y' which is a very competitive school.
